The Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance, raising it at the low end, and said earnings next year will be in line with its results from this year. Ford has been working to recover production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year. In this article F Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:55 01:55 Ford reports mixed third-quarter results, says 2027 earnings will be in line with this year Today's Videos DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter. The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year. "This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday. Ford reported third-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $4.7 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than what analysts were anticipating, according to StreetAccount. Here's how Ford performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 49 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expected Automotive revenue: $46.08 billion vs. $46.24 billion expected The Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance to adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10.5 billion and $11 billion, compared with a previous outlook of $10 billion to $11 billion. Ford maintained its adjusted free cash flow guidance for this year of between $6 billion and $7 billion. House said the company expects 2027 earnings to be roughly in line with this year's results, citing several offsetting factors in production issues this year as well as rising commodity costs. House noted a $1.3 billion tariff refund during the first quarter of this year was largely offset by additional costs from alternative aluminum sourcing that the company does not expect to have next year, leveling out the year-over-year comparison. She also said production of its F-Series Super Duty trucks in Canada in 2027 will make up for lost production it's expecting at its F-150 factories to retool for new models. "Next year will be the third year on our journey of increasing and improving our warranty and material cost savings, and that's getting extended to structural costs throughout the company as well in terms of savings," House said. Ford CEO Jim Farley called 2027 a "foundational year" for the company on its way to a previously announced target of an 8% adjusted EBIT margin by 2029. The company reported a 5.4% margin during the third quarter. Ahead of the results, Wall Street analysts were mixed about whether Ford would be able to maintain profits in 2027. The company has multiple efforts that will add to costs next year: It's rolling out several new or redesigned models, including its next-generation EV and Canada-produced pickups, and is enhancing its energy business that it announced earlier this year. The missed revenue for the third quarter was a result of each of the automaker's main business units – which are broken into Blue traditional operations, Pro fleet and Model e electric vehicle segments – underperforming compared with Wall Street's expectations, according to StreetAccount. As part of its modified guidance, Ford said it now expects pre-tax earnings of its Ford Blue unit to be $5.5 billion, which is at the high end of a previous guidance. It's also anticipating EBIT of about $7 billion for the year for Ford Pro and Ford Model e losses of about $4 billion. Its Ford Credit unit is expected to record about $2.8 billion in EBIT for 2026. Ford's overall revenue, which includes its credit segment, was off roughly 2% compared with the third quarter of last year, to $49.5 billion. Its net income also was off $400 million from a year earlier to $2 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes were up slightly year-over-year to $2.7 billion. Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted. headlines.article_text: Microsoft (MSFT) Q1 earnings report 2027 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft reported 19% revenue growth, topping estimates. Azure cloud revenue jumped 48% to $33.2 billion. Free cash flow declined 27% from a year ago. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella speaks at a company event at La Defense business district in Puteaux, near Paris, on Oct. 20, 2026. Dimitar Dilkoff | AFP | Getty Images Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus: Earnings per share: $4.89 adjusted vs. $4.73 expected Revenue: $92.28 billion vs. $90.69 billion expected Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business. The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion. Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases." Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue. Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time. Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%. Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses. In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services. The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on a conference call with analysts. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers. Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand. As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities. Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET. This story is developing. Please check back for updates. headlines.article_text: DoorDash's deal to buy Instacart coming as early as Thursday morning, sources tell CNBC Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points DoorDash's bid to buy Instacart could be announced as early as Thursday morning, CNBC has learned. Speculation of a deal has swirled since last week, and several outlets reported the acquisition could value Instacart at roughly $17 billion. watch now VIDEO 1:02 01:02 DoorDash deal to buy Instacart to be announced as early as Thursday morning Closing Bell: Overtime DoorDash 's bid to buy Instacart could be announced as soon as Thursday morning, sources familiar with the matter told CNBC. Speculation of a deal has swirled since last week, when The Information reported Instacart was exploring a sale and had held talks with companies including Uber and DoorDash. On Monday, several outlets reported DoorDash was in advanced discussions to acquire Instacart and that the deal could value Instacart at about $17 billion. Instacart's stock popped about 4% in extended trading on Wednesday, while DoorDash shares fell less than 1%. Acquiring Instacart would give DoorDash a bigger presence in online grocery delivery. DoorDash got its start in food delivery, and since then it has added more retailers to its marketplace, such as Sephora, Macy's , Staples and Anthropologie. In recent months, it's brought on a growing stable of regional grocers, after announcing a partnership with Kroger last year. Instacart , which went public in 2023, was one of the biggest beneficiaries of a pandemic-driven surge in grocery delivery services, but it has struggled to maintain that momentum amid stiffer competition from companies like Amazon and Walmart . After slowing its brick-and-mortar grocery effort, Amazon has doubled down on its online grocery business and leveraged its vast fulfillment footprint to speed up deliveries of household essentials, pantry staples and perishables. Both Amazon and Walmart have pushed further into same- and next-day delivery, which poses a threat to Instacart's on-demand delivery model. Analysts have noted that a potential combination of Instacart and DoorDash could attract antitrust scrutiny given the companies' market overlap. "3P delivery platforms remain a minority of total grocery consumption, but slicing and dicing the online market more narrowly or from a perspective of the grocers as enterprise customers can make approvals more challenging," Wedbush analysts wrote in a Monday research note. In this article GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:00 01:00 Alphabet shares fall on Q3 revenue miss Closing Bell: Overtime Alphabet shares slumped more than 10% after the search giant reported a drop in free cash flow during the third quarter in a worrying sign for the artificial intelligence trade. Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share : $2.67 adjusted vs. $3.02 expected Revenue: $127.58 billion vs. $128.22 billion Revenue grew 25% from a year ago, but the company posted its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years. Net income fell to $26.17 billion, or $2.12 per share, down from $34.98 billion, or $2.87 per share. Google's reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, which fell far further than the $2.70 billion expected by analysts. As questions mount over heightened spending on the artificial intelligence buildout, Google's capital expenditures totaled $51.36 billion, falling short of the $55.09 billion expected by analysts. Investors are looking for a substantial return on investment to warrant its big spending plans. Alphabet maintained its full-year capital expenditures forecast after lifting guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion during the second quarter from $190 billion. Annual capex is expected to top $200 billion before exceeding $300 billion in 2027. "We continue to expect our capex to increase significantly in 2027, and will provide further details on our Q4 call," finance chief Anat Ashkenazi told analysts during an earnings call. The company's borrowing rose sharply during the quarter, with long-term debt climbing to $125.1 billion, up from $21.6 billion a year earlier — an increase of about 479%. Operating income totaled $40.58 billion, missing a $43.19 billion forecast from FactSet. Alphabet saw a $99.03 billion windfall in revenue from equity holdings in the second quarter, fueled by stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic. However, the category weighed on results in the third quarter, resulting in loss of $8.66 billion. Google continues to open its wallet to fuel the AI expansion. That contributed to strong revenue growth in its cloud division, home to its suit of AI offerings. "We are seeing extraordinary demand and strong growth from both AI labs, capital markets, financial service institutions, and enterprises," said Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian in his first public earnings remarks. Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, surpassing the $28.7 billion, or 90% growth expected by analysts. The company continues taking market share from larger rivals Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. The strong cloud results did little to shake off Google's negative print. "The cloud business was the only business that beat at 103% growth, said Jefferies analyst Brent Thill on CNBC's Closing Bell: Overtime. "The Street wanted 100%, so it didn't beat by much, and it missed some of the high-end targets. Everything else missed." The company's aggressive push on its AI models also showed signs of a payoff. Google said its Gemini app reached 1 billion users, making it the fastest-growing product in its history. CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts that the company is already seeing strong demand for its recently launched Argon Gemini model. Its Carbon iteration announced on Wednesday outperforms Argon "on almost every domain," he added. Alphabet's search revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion. That fell short of a $64.96 billion estimate. Pichai said the company's AI investments powered the highest query growth rate over the last five years. Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: Alphabet, Microsoft, Chipotle, ServiceNow, Fortinet & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: GOOGL, MSFT, CMG, NOW Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading. Maplebear — The company that owns Instacart gained 3% after sources familiar with the matter told CNBC that DoorDash's deal to buy the delivery service could arrive as soon as Thursday morning. DoorDash fell about 1%. Chipotle Mexican Grill — Shares gained more than 5% after the burrito chain reported same-store sales that beat estimates. Same-store sales in the third quarter grew 2.1%, versus the 1.5% increase analysts polled by FactSet anticipated. ServiceNow — The enterprise software company tumbled 15%. Third-quarter adjusted profit of $1 per share missed the LSEG consensus expectation of $1.02 a share Subscription revenue guidance for the fourth quarter ranged from $4.245 billion to $4.255 billion, while the FactSet consensus called for $4.25 billion. Fortinet — The cybersecurity company plummeted 25%. Non-GAAP gross margin for the third quarter came in at 79.6%, while analysts polled by LSEG sought 80.1%. Separately, top- and bottom-line results beat the Street's expectations. Microsoft – The software giant rose 2% after the company reported a beat on the top and bottom lines for its fiscal first-quarter earnings. Revenue came in at $92.28 billion, ahead of the $90.69 billion expected by LSEG. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share was better than the $4.73 expected by analysts. Revenue in the mega-cap's key Azure cloud business grew 48% year over year. Alphabet – Shares of the Google parent are down 9% in extended trading Wednesday after its third-quarter earnings showed the company posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion. Its core search revenue of $63.35 billion, missed the $64.96 billion estimate from analysts. Total company revenue of $127.58 billion also missed LSEG expectations of $128.22 billion. Align Technology — The maker of orthodontics and aesthetic dentistry products dropped 1% after fourth-quarter revenue guidance missed analysts' consensus estimates, according to FactSet data. The company also named Procter & Gamble alumna Jennifer Davis as its new CEO, effective Dec. 31. Sprouts Farmers Market — The Phoenix-based grocery chain plunged 18% after third-quarter earnings per share, revenue and same-store sales all trailed analysts' consensus estimates, according to FactSet data. Ford Motor — Shares fell nearly 2% after hours. The company reported third-quarter earnings that beat Wall Street's estimates but slightly missed on revenue. Adjusted earnings of 49 cents a share topped the LSEG consensus estimate of 40 cents per share, while revenue of $46.08 billion narrowly missed the $46.24 billion expected. FedEx — Shares fell almost 2% even as the delivery giant reported third quarter adjusted earnings that beat expectations. FedEx also said expects its full-year revenue growth at 12% year over year, up from the earlier call for an increase of roughly 11%, supported by stronger pricing and improved shipment volumes. Honeywell Aerospace — The aerospace company was down more than 2% even after raising its full-year outlook for pro forma standalone adjusted earnings per share, calling for $7.85 to $8. The company also announced an initial quarterly cash dividend of 40 cents per share. Carvana — The used car dealer climbed 10%. Carvana third-quarter revenue and adjusted EBITDA topped the numbers Wall Street had been expecting, and it said the Securities and Exchange Commission closed a previously disclosed investigation and would not take any enforcement action. CNBC's Paulina Likos, Scott Schnipper, Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

headlines.article_text: FedEx (FDX) Sept 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points FedEx on Wednesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third-quarter results. The company also raised its full-year guidance. It's FedEx's first earnings report since the company realigned its fiscal year, moving year-end from May 31 to Dec. 31. In this article FDX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A FedEx delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on July 25, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty Images FedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earnings that beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines and raised its full-year outlook for its newly realigned fiscal year. Shares of the company fell slightly in extended trading. Here's how the company performed for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.74 adjusted vs. $3.36 expected Revenue: $22.86 billion vs. $22.42 billion expected The company reported net income for the quarter of $290 million, or $1.21 per share, compared with $650 million, or $2.73 per share, during the comparable period a year prior. Adjusting for one-time items — including losses related to short-term investments, gains on the extinguishment of debt and certain restructuring costs — FedEx reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.74. It marks the first report of FedEx's realigned fiscal year, moving the end of its calendar from May 31 to Dec. 31. The report also comes after the company successfully spun out FedEx Freight into a separate publicly traded company. FedEx said its express U.S. segment operating income increased in the quarter, primarily driven by higher package yields and volume. "As our strong operating results and adjusted free cash flow demonstrate, FedEx is winning across high-value market segments while we optimize our network, driving an increase to our full-year outlook," CEO Raj Subramaniam said in a statement. For the full year, the company is now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $18 and $18.60, compared to a prior range of $16.90 to $18.10. FedEx also said it's revising its 2026 revenue growth expectation to a roughly 12% year-over-year increase, up from previous guidance of an 11% increase. Earlier this week, FedEx named former AutoZone exec Jamere Jackson as the company's new chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. He replaces Claude Russ, who served as the interim CFO since June 1. John Dietrich was announced as stepping down from that role in April. headlines.summary: Apple announces a new touchscreen laptop, the company's third major launch under new CEO John Ternus.
headlines.article_text: MacBook Pro: Apple brings touch to the Mac Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple announced its first laptop with a touchscreen will go on sale Nov. 6. The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. Global PC shipments have fallen and Apple faces pressure from rising memory costs and higher computer prices. Touchscreens have not typically driven laptop purchases, making Apple's software changes and developer strategy central to whether the feature catches on. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT German-Russian record producer and DJ Zedd, at left, and Apple CEO John Ternus look at the new M6 14-inch MacBook Pro during the Apple Experience LA event in Los Angeles, Oct. 28, 2026. Frederic J. Brown | Afp | Getty Images Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display. Apple said the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current Pro laptops. It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid. The new laptop will go on sale Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models. This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases. It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature. "Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles. The laptop market has been going through one of its worst slumps ever. Overall shipments are expected to be down 11% this year. Analysts say the AI-driven global market shortage of memory has contributed to higher laptop prices, which has hurt sales and demand. In the third quarter, total PC shipments dropped 20% on a year-over-year basis, according to market researcher IDC. Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate. Attendees try out the new touchscreen MacBook Pro during the Apple Experience LA in Los Angeles, Oct. 28, 2026. Frederic J. Brown | AFP | Getty Images Even Apple's not immune to rising memory prices, after then-CEO Tim Cook warned this summer that the situation around memory prices was "unsustainable." Nearly all Macs got price hikes this year. Mac Minis introduced in August got a $300 bump, for example. The announcement caps a busy two months of product launches under Ternus. Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June. Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor. In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions. The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue. But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps. And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud. Meta's AI model developer team bought hundreds of Mac Minis this year to test agents, for example. And Apple notably teamed up with Meta earlier this month to make an announcement that large, nearly frontier models can run on clusters of Macs connected with high-speed cabling, allowing developers to run agentic code without paying Anthropic or OpenAI. Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021. "It's totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven't really felt a reason to change that." Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's. Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement . That may be why Ternus in his early days as CEO will be the executive to backtrack on a long-running Apple design philosophy. Touchscreen laptops have been available on Windows machines for a long time, but they're just another feature, not a selling point behind most purchasing decisions, said Ryan Reith, IDC's vice president for worldwide device trackers. Only 17% of notebook PCs shipped globally this year will have touchscreens, according to IDC data. Touchscreen laptops also have a slightly lower average selling price than non-touchscreen notebooks. Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop. "This is really a user interface and software thing," Reith said. headlines.summary: President Donald Trump banned MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House in September, only to have a judge he appointed order their return.
headlines.article_text: Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points MS NOW, CNN and Politico, in an amended lawsuit, asked a judge to order that they be allowed to serve as press pool for areas in the White House such as the Oval Office, as well as on Air Force One. President Trump banned the media outlets from the White House in September, but a federal judge soon afterward ordered that they be readmitted there. The outlets say the White House has continued to prevent them from coverage certain areas of the complex. The amended complaint sets the stage for a court fight over whether a president, because of how he or she feels about how a media outlet covers them, can block access to individual media outlets or reporters from areas of the White House that other journalists have access to. In this article VSNT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT U.S. President Donald Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. Alex Wong | Getty Images Three media outlets that President Donald Trump banned from the White House in September, only to have a federal judge's order restore much of their access, amended their lawsuit Wednesday, seeking to regain full access to serve in a press pool for other reporters in the Oval Office and Air Force One . The amended civil complaint against Trump says that since the judge ordered the White House to allow MS NOW , CNN and Politico journalists into the White House, the White House has blocked those outlets from performing pool functions they long have conducted. The press pool routinely serves as a key source of information for the public about what a president does or says. In pool assignments, journalists agree to share with other media outlets information and images they obtain while acting as a pooler. The amended complaint sets the stage for a court fight over whether a president, because of how he or she feels about how a media outlet covers them, can block access to individual media outlets or reporters from areas of the White House that other journalists have access to. Ted Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, in a statement Wednesday said, "Despite two court orders restraining it from implementing the President's unconstitutional ban on CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, the White House has continued to violate the First Amendment and due process by excluding those news organizations from areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One — the very locations that the President most frequently engages with the press." "These exclusions, intended to punish and chill coverage of the administration that the President doesn't like, make it harder for the press to cover some of the most important events in the world for the benefit of the American people," Boutrous said. The amended complaint in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C. says that Trump's original ban and "the White House's continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain [areas] are unlawful retaliation for protected First Amendment activity." Those actions "brazenly" discriminate against the outlets "based on their perceived editorial viewpoint; the White House is expressly excluding CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO because the President dislikes the content of their coverage," the suit says. Judge Tim Kelly's prior orders restoring access for the outlets did not require the White House to restore those outlets' access to the Oval Office or Air Force One. The amended complaint notes that since his second term began in January 2025, Trump has held 121 press events aboard Air Force One or on the tarmac outside the presidential plane, and 138 events in the Oval Office, "during which he fielded no fewer than 4,700 questions from reporters." "To be clear, Plaintiffs do not claim an unrestricted right to enter the Oval Office or travel aboard Air Force One," the new complaint says. "But once the White House opens those spaces to selected journalists for newsgathering and reporting, the White House may not exclude Plaintiffs because it dislikes their coverage." Members of the media report from Pebble Beach, the stand-up area for members of the media on the North Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty Images Since Trump announced the ban on Sept. 18, "the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from fulfilling its duties as designated television network pooler aboard Air Force One — a role CNN has fulfilled for more than four decades," the amended suit says. MS NOW has not participated in the secondary TV pool since that date, and the White House has barred Politico "from two scheduled out-of-town print pool assignments aboard Air Force One," the suit says. "Defendants have offered no official explanation for any of these exclusions," the amended complaint says. "Indeed, the President has been explicit that he intends to limit access to the Oval Office to news organizations that cover him favorably, declaring hours after this action was filed that 'publications that only write negatively . . . shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," the suit said. The suit notes that after Kelly issued a preliminary injunction against Trump's ban in mid-October, "the White House issued a statement declaring that what it deems the 'Fake News' has 'no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office.'" President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One en route to Alaska on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty Images The amended complaint says the limited ban on pool access violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution. "CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO, and their journalists have liberty and property interests in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford to the White House grounds to report on the President and his administration," the suit says. "That access has long extended to the Oval Office, Air Force One, and other fora that the White House has opened to the press for pool coverage." "The ban, and Defendants' continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain White House press areas, deprives Plaintiffs of those interests without meeting the bare minimum requirements of due process: advance notice based on clear standards and an opportunity to be heard," the suit says. The suit also said the White House is interfering with CNN's ability to perform its duties as one of five television networks that "staff, equip, and bear the costs associated with the primary television network pool upon which the American public (and the White House itself) relies for real-time television coverage of the President in the Oval Office, aboard Air Force One, and at the many other presidential events that due to size and other constraints simply cannot accommodate all members of the press corps." Trump, when he announced the ban, said he was "sick" of what he called fiction and lies written about him, his administration, and the United States.
